# Before running the analysis

Download `ETFs.csv` and `MutualFunds.csv` from
<https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stefanoleone992/mutual-funds-and-etfs>
and put both files in `data/`.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
# dplyr and tidyr are included in tidyverse. tools.R contains the project's
# allocation and diagnostic functions.
library(tidyverse)
source("tools.R")
```

## 1. Prepare the model data

```{r clean-data}
# Keep the response, adjustment variables, and raw P/E for the missingness audit.
columns <- c(
  "fund_return_ytd", "fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio",
  "total_net_assets", "inception_date", "asset_stocks", "asset_bonds",
  "annual_holdings_turnover", "fund_price_earning_ratio",
  "fund_sector_technology"
)

read_funds <- function(path, is_etf) {
  data <- read.csv(path, na.strings = c("", "NA"))

  # tools.R fills an unknown allocation with zero when the known allocations
  # already total 100%, or with the remaining share when exactly one is missing.
  # Apply this before selecting columns: the rule needs every asset_* column.
  asset_columns <- grep("^asset_", names(data), value = TRUE)
  data <- impute_allocation(data, asset_columns)

  data <- data[columns]
  data$etf_indicator <- as.integer(is_etf) # 1 = ETF; 0 = mutual fund
  data
}

funds <- bind_rows(
  read_funds("data/ETFs.csv", TRUE),
  read_funds("data/MutualFunds.csv", FALSE)
)

# Use January 1, 2021 as the age reference. The date filter excludes funds
# that had not yet started by then; missing dates are excluded as well.
funds <- funds |>
  mutate(inception_date = as.Date(inception_date)) |>
  filter(inception_date < as.Date("2021-01-01")) |>
  mutate(fund_age_years = as.numeric(
    as.Date("2021-01-01") - inception_date
  ) / 365.25) |>
  select(-inception_date)

# A missing P/E is not zero. Use two terms so such funds can stay in the
# model: pe_reported identifies whether P/E was supplied; the centered term
# is zero for missing P/E and equals P/E minus the sample median otherwise.
median_pe <- median(funds$fund_price_earning_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
funds <- funds |>
  mutate(
    pe_reported = as.integer(!is.na(fund_price_earning_ratio)),
    pe_centered_when_reported = coalesce(fund_price_earning_ratio, median_pe) - median_pe
  )

# Retain raw P/E in funds for the audit. It is not a model column because
# requiring it to be complete would discard the observations above.
model_data <- funds |>
  select(-fund_price_earning_ratio) |>
  drop_na()
```

### Sample and missingness audit

```{r sample-audit}
fund_type <- function(x) factor(x, levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("Mutual fund", "ETF"))

# table() counts each fund type; the third row counts fitted records with P/E.
sample_counts <- rbind(
  "Eligible after inception filter" = table(fund_type(funds$etf_indicator)),
  "Main model sample" = table(fund_type(model_data$etf_indicator)),
  "P/E reported in model sample" = table(fund_type(
    model_data$etf_indicator[model_data$pe_reported == 1]
  ))
)
knitr::kable(cbind(sample_counts, Total = rowSums(sample_counts)))

retained_pct <- 100 * sample_counts["Main model sample", ] /
  sample_counts["Eligible after inception filter", ]
knitr::kable(rbind("Eligible records retained (%)" = round(retained_pct, 1)))

# Count missing values before complete-case filtering. This shows which
# fields cause sample loss, separately for ETFs and mutual funds.
audit_columns <- c(setdiff(columns, "inception_date"), "fund_age_years")
missing_by_type <- sapply(
  split(funds[audit_columns], fund_type(funds$etf_indicator)),
  function(group) colSums(is.na(group))
)
knitr::kable(missing_by_type)
```

Allocation filling uses the unit-sum rule in `tools.R`. The missingness
table describes records after that step. Unequal retention by fund type
limits how broadly the fitted sample can represent either population.

## 2. Fit the main model

```{r regression}
model <- lm(
  fund_return_ytd ~ total_net_assets + fund_age_years +
    asset_stocks + asset_bonds + annual_holdings_turnover +
    fund_sector_technology + pe_reported + pe_centered_when_reported +
    fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio * etf_indicator,
  data = model_data
)
fitted_data <- model.frame(model) # Exact rows and variables used by lm().
summary(model)
confint(model)
```

The `*` includes the expense ratio, the ETF indicator, and their interaction.
The ETF coefficient is the adjusted ETF–mutual fund difference at an expense
ratio of zero. The interaction is the difference between their expense-ratio
slopes. These coefficients are associations, not causal effects.

```{r partial-tests}
# Each F test removes one term from the full model while keeping the others.
drop1(model, test = "F")
```

## 3. Diagnostics

```{r diagnostics, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# tools.R computes Cook's distance, DFFITS, DFBETAS, leverage, and course
# screening cutoffs. It also prints flagged observations and model VIFs when
# the car package is installed. The model fit itself does not need car.
checks <- check_model(model, plots = FALSE)
plots <- model_plots(model, point_cex = 0.8,
  diagnostics = checks$diagnostics, cutoffs = checks$cutoffs)
plots$presentation_plot()
```

```{r export-diagnostics}
# Keep the model variables and diagnostics together, in fitted-row order.
# CSV is readable by Excel and does not require an extra export package.
diagnostic_data <- cbind(
  original_row = checks$diagnostics$row_id,
  fitted_data,
  checks$diagnostics[c("cooks", "dffits", "dfbetas",
    "residuals", "leverage", "flags")]
)
write.csv(diagnostic_data, "model_data_diagnostics.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## 4. Exploratory checks

### Return by fund type

```{r return-by-type}
# Returns are stored as proportions; multiply by 100 for percentages.
returns_by_type <- split(100 * fitted_data$fund_return_ytd,
  fund_type(fitted_data$etf_indicator))
return_summary <- t(vapply(returns_by_type, function(y) {
  c(n = length(y), median_return_pct = median(y), sd_return_pct = sd(y))
}, numeric(3)))
knitr::kable(return_summary, digits = 2)
```

### Trial transformations

The models below use the **same observations**. Logging assets changes a
predictor's scale. The square-root and log trials change the response scale,
so their coefficient values and fitted responses are not directly comparable
to the original model's.

```{r transformations, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
# The transformations need positive inputs. Stop with a clear error if the
# data do not meet that requirement.
stopifnot(all(fitted_data$total_net_assets > 0),
  all(1 + fitted_data$fund_return_ytd > 0))

log_assets_model <- update(model,
  . ~ . - total_net_assets + log(total_net_assets),
  data = fitted_data, na.action = na.fail)
sqrt_return_model <- update(log_assets_model,
  sqrt(1 + fund_return_ytd) ~ .)
log_return_model <- update(log_assets_model,
  log(1 + fund_return_ytd) ~ .)

# Standardized residuals divide each residual by its estimated standard
# deviation. The smooth curve highlights patterns; Q-Q points assess tails.
plot_residuals <- function(fit, title) {
  r <- rstandard(fit)
  x <- fitted(fit)
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  plot(x, r, pch = ".", main = title,
    xlab = "Fitted response", ylab = "Standardized residual")
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey50")
  lines(lowess(x, r), col = "firebrick")
  qqnorm(r, pch = ".")
  qqline(r, col = "firebrick")
}

trial_models <- list(original = model, log_assets = log_assets_model,
  sqrt_return = sqrt_return_model, log_return = log_return_model)
for (name in names(trial_models)) plot_residuals(trial_models[[name]], name)

# Compare standardized-residual spread at low and high fitted values.
# cut() forms ten equal-count groups, so the first and last describe the ends.
residual_spread <- function(fit) {
  r <- rstandard(fit)
  groups <- cut(fitted(fit),
    breaks = quantile(fitted(fit), 0:10 / 10), include.lowest = TRUE)
  spread <- tapply(r, groups, sd)
  c(low_sd = spread[1], high_sd = spread[10],
    lower_tail = unname(quantile(r, 0.01)))
}
knitr::kable(t(vapply(trial_models, residual_spread, numeric(3))), digits = 2)
```

### Box–Cox profile

```{r boxcox, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Box–Cox requires a positive response. Adding 1 is valid for these fitted
# returns; profiling lambda then tests possible power transformations.
positive_model <- update(model, I(1 + fund_return_ytd) ~ .,
  data = fitted_data, na.action = na.fail, y = TRUE)
profile <- MASS::boxcox(positive_model,
  lambda = seq(-2, 3, by = 0.01), plotit = FALSE, interp = FALSE)
peak <- which.max(profile$y)
lambda_hat <- profile$x[peak]

# For one profiled parameter, the likelihood-ratio 95% region lies no more
# than qchisq(.95, 1)/2 below the maximum log-likelihood.
cutoff <- profile$y[peak] - qchisq(0.95, df = 1) / 2
lambda_ci <- range(profile$x[profile$y >= cutoff])
plot(profile$x, profile$y, type = "l", xlab = expression(lambda),
  ylab = "Profile log-likelihood", main = "Box–Cox: original predictors")
abline(h = cutoff, col = "red", lty = 2)
abline(v = lambda_hat, col = "blue", lty = 2)
c(estimate = lambda_hat, lower = lambda_ci[1], upper = lambda_ci[2])
```

### P/E terms and allocation collinearity

```{r pe-and-vif}
# Compare nested models on exactly the same rows. This partial F test asks
# whether the P/E reporting indicator and centered P/E help jointly.
without_pe <- update(model,
  . ~ . - pe_reported - pe_centered_when_reported,
  data = fitted_data, na.action = na.fail)
anova(without_pe, model)

# VIF = 1/(1 - R^2) from regressing one predictor on all other design
# columns. Report the two allocation variables of interest. This avoids a
# package dependency and uses the actual columns in each fitted model.
allocation_vif <- function(fit) {
  x <- model.matrix(fit)[, -1, drop = FALSE] # Remove the intercept column.
  vapply(c("asset_stocks", "asset_bonds"), function(variable) {
    other <- x[, colnames(x) != variable, drop = FALSE]
    r2 <- summary(lm(x[, variable] ~ other))$r.squared
    1 / (1 - r2)
  }, numeric(1))
}
knitr::kable(rbind(
  original = allocation_vif(model),
  log_assets = allocation_vif(log_assets_model),
  without_pe = allocation_vif(without_pe)
), digits = 2)
```

Unequal residual variance weakens the usual partial F-test interpretation.
The VIF measures collinearity among model columns, not whether allocations
are measured accurately.

### Sensitivity to the largest Cook's distance

```{r influence-sensitivity}
# Cook's distance combines leverage and residual size. Removing its largest
# observation is a sensitivity check, not a reason to delete that fund.
largest_row <- which.max(checks$diagnostics$cooks)
c(max_cook = checks$diagnostics$cooks[largest_row],
  cook_cutoff = checks$cutoffs[["cooks"]],
  high_leverage = sum(checks$diagnostics$high_leverage),
  abs_standardized_residual_over_4 = sum(abs(rstandard(model)) > 4))

fitted_data[largest_row, c("etf_indicator", "fund_return_ytd",
  "fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio"), drop = FALSE]
without_largest <- lm(formula(model),
  data = fitted_data[-largest_row, ], na.action = na.fail)
interaction <- "fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio:etf_indicator"
c(full = unname(coef(model)[interaction]),
  without_largest = unname(coef(without_largest)[interaction]))
```
